strengths: The paper offers a clean conceptual framing that unifies several existing lines of work (TMPD/DPS-variants and optimization-based solvers like DiffPIR/DCDP/DMPlug) under a single 'local MAP' perspective, clarifying when local-MAP updates coincide with posterior-mean-based DPS updates (Gaussian conditional case) and when they diverge.

The 2D Gaussian-mixture toy example (Fig. 3, Appendix A) is a nice, interpretable illustration that concretely shows the mode-seeking vs. mode-averaging behavior of local MAP vs. DPS/DAPS, which supports the qualitative claims made in Sec. 3.2.

Very broad empirical evaluation: 10 image restoration tasks (linear, nonlinear, non-differentiable) on FFHQ/ImageNet plus 3 scientific inverse-problem benchmarks (LIS, CS-MRI, black hole imaging), with comparisons against a large number of competitive baselines (DPS, DAPS, SITCOM, DiffPIR, DCDP, PnP-DM, RED-diff, etc.).

Strong and fairly consistent quantitative improvements (best in 49/60 image-restoration cases, best PSNR on all scientific tasks), often achieved with lower computational cost/NFEs than the strongest baselines (DAPS, SITCOM), as shown in the runtime ablation (Table 3, Fig. 4).

Practical contributions are useful: an interpretable convex-combination reformulation of the local MAP objective with automatic annealing behavior, and a simple, effective surrogate-gradient trick for non-differentiable forward operators (JPEG, quantization) that is shown to clearly outperform ΠGDM on these tasks.

Reasonable reproducibility support: explicit algorithm pseudocode (Algorithm 4), a full hyperparameter table (Table 4) across all 20 task settings, dataset/license details, and extensive qualitative visualizations in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core theoretical contribution is fairly thin: the main formal fact used throughout (local MAP = DPS mean iff the conditional posterior p(x0|xt,y) is Gaussian) is an elementary observation, and no result establishes convergence, error bounds, or a precise characterization of when/how much the local-MAP trajectory deviates from either the global MAP or the true posterior in the nonlinear, non-Gaussian regime that dominates the experiments.

The proposed 'probabilistically interpretable' covariance Σ0|t ≈ (k/SNR)I (Sec 4.1) is itself a loose heuristic justified only by qualitative bounds/limits (1)-(3), and the paper explicitly shows it is mathematically equivalent to the heuristic λt-weighted objective used by prior optimization-based methods (Eq. 14 vs Eq. 11 with Σ0|t=λtσy^2 I). The claimed gain in 'interpretability' is therefore largely a re-parameterization; the paper asserts (but does not rigorously ablate) that this reparameterization is what drives the empirical gains.

No direct ablation isolating the effect of the objective reformulation (Eq. 13) versus the mathematically equivalent original formulation (Eq. 14) with well-tuned λt is provided, despite the paper explicitly claiming 'empirical performance strongly depends on our objective reformulation' — this central methodological claim is unverified.

Closely related prior work (Xu et al. [32], which also argues DPS is better understood as MAP estimation, and Gutha et al. [12], which targets global MAP with diffusion priors) is discussed only briefly in related work and is not included as an empirical baseline, despite apparent conceptual overlap with the paper's central thesis.

Some result inconsistencies/possible errors: Table 1 reports unusually large SSIM/LPIPS standard deviations for the Quantization task (e.g., SSIM 0.844±0.467, LPIPS 0.229±0.474), which appear anomalous or possibly mis-tabulated and are not discussed, raising minor concerns about result curation/checking.

The claimed 'best in 49/60 cases' is true but obscures that SITCOM outperforms LMAPS on several ImageNet settings (SR 4×, Inpaint Box, Nonlinear Deblurring); the narrative in the main text emphasizes wins without proportionate discussion of where and why the method underperforms.

Minor presentation/consistency issues: Algorithm 4 and Table 3 refer to the method as 'MAPS' rather than 'LMAPS'; some hyperparameter table entries contain typos (e.g., '0..01' in Table 4); the abstract's headline PSNR gains are cherry-picked from a subset of tasks.

strengths: Broad and fairly comprehensive empirical evaluation: 10 image-restoration tasks (linear, nonlinear, non-differentiable) on FFHQ/ImageNet plus 3 scientific inverse problems (LIS, CS-MRI, black-hole imaging), compared against a long list of strong baselines (DPS, DAPS, SITCOM, DiffPIR, DCDP, PnP-DM, RED-diff, etc.).

The paper attempts a useful conceptual clarification of the relationship between posterior-mean-based conditional generation (DPS), posterior sampling, and optimization-based 'data-consistency' solvers, situating many existing methods (TMPD, DDNM, IIGDM, DiffPIR, DCDP) as special cases of a common local-MAP template (Eq. 8, 11-14).

The gradient surrogate for non-differentiable forward operators (JPEG quantization, bit quantization) is simple and practically useful, and the paper demonstrates sizeable gains (>2dB) on these previously under-addressed tasks.
Reasonably thorough appendix with hyperparameters, licenses, additional metrics, timing comparisons, and visualizations, aiding some reproducibility.
weaknesses: Internal inconsistency undermines confidence in the reported results: the abstract states LMAPS achieves the best results in '46/60' cases while Section 5.2 states '49 out of 60' for the identical comparison — such a discrepancy suggests insufficient proofreading/verification of the headline empirical claim.

The central theoretical contribution is largely a negative/deflationary result dressed as a unifying framework: Section 3.2 explicitly shows that local MAP sampling neither samples the true posterior (except in the Gaussian special case) nor provably converges to the global MAP. The 'unification' therefore mostly restates that these methods are ad hoc compromises, without providing new guarantees, bounds, or conditions characterizing when/why the trade-off is favorable.

The core methodological novelty (Sec. 4.1's isotropic covariance choice and the reformulated objective in Eq. 13) is explicitly acknowledged to be mathematically equivalent to the existing heuristic objective of prior optimization-based methods (Eq. 14); the paper asserts that 'empirical performance strongly depends on the objective reformulation' but provides no ablation isolating this effect from other design choices (learning rate, per-task tuning, number of gradient/annealing steps), so this claim is unverified.

For linear inverse problems (Sec. 4.2), a closed-form solution is derived (Eq. 15) yet the method still runs K steps of gradient descent 'despite the availability of the closed form,' which is not well motivated and undercuts the claimed principled/efficient nature of the approach.

Extensive per-task hyperparameter tuning (Table 4 lists distinct k1, k2, learning rate, and step counts for every one of ~20 tasks) raises concerns about overfitting to specific benchmarks and about the practical usability/generalizability of the method without similarly extensive tuning on new tasks.

Ablation studies are narrow: Figure 4 only studies optimization-steps-vs-NFE trade-offs for a single task (Gaussian deblurring); there is no ablation decomposing the contributions of the three proposed components (covariance approximation, objective reformulation, gradient surrogate) individually, despite each being presented as a distinct contribution.

Many main-table results lack standard deviations/uncertainty estimates (only nonlinear tasks report them), and baseline numbers are taken from prior papers under potentially different protocols/budgets, making some comparisons in Tables 1-2 not fully apples-to-apples (e.g., differing NFE budgets in Table 3).

The method is closely related to prior work explicitly cited (Xu et al. [32], which also argues DPS is closer to MAP estimation, and Gutha et al. [12], which proposes global MAP sampling for diffusion); the differentiation from these closely related works is only briefly discussed in one sentence in Related Work, without deeper technical or empirical comparison.

LMAPS is not uniformly state-of-the-art even in the paper's own tables (e.g., SITCOM outperforms LMAPS on several ImageNet tasks such as SR 4x, Inpaint-Box, and Nonlinear Deblurring), which is understated relative to the strong 'state-of-the-art' framing in the abstract.

strengths: The paper provides a clear conceptual taxonomy that positions optimization-based inverse problem solvers (DiffPIR, DCDP, DMPlug, etc.) as instances of a 'local MAP' step within the diffusion trajectory, clarifying their relationship to DPS-style posterior sampling and to TMPD; the Gaussian-mixture and 2D toy examples (Sec. 3, Appendix A) nicely illustrate the mode-seeking vs. mode-averaging distinction.

Practically motivated methodological contributions: an isotropic covariance approximation that avoids the expensive Jacobian-vector product required by TMPD, a scale-invariant convex-combination reformulation of the local MAP objective with interpretable annealing behavior, and a simple surrogate-gradient trick that extends the framework to non-differentiable forward operators (JPEG, quantization).

Broad empirical coverage: 10 image-restoration tasks (linear, nonlinear, non-differentiable) on FFHQ/ImageNet plus 3 scientific inverse problems (linear inverse scattering, CS-MRI, black-hole imaging), compared against a large and current set of baselines (DAPS, SITCOM, PnP-DM, RED-diff, etc.).

Favorable efficiency profile: Table 3 and Figure 4 show LMAPS reaching performance comparable to or better than DAPS/SITCOM with substantially fewer NFEs, which is a meaningful practical advantage if it holds broadly.
Reasonable reproducibility support: full hyperparameter table (Table 4), dataset/license details, and extensive qualitative visualizations are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The 'unification' is largely definitional (swap the conditional mean for the conditional mode in the same DDIM update) rather than a deep theoretical result, and the paper itself concedes local MAP neither samples the posterior nor converges to the global MAP outside the Gaussian case—so the promised 'principled interpretation' for optimization-based methods is fairly loose and the practical algorithm still relies on heuristic choices (isotropic covariance, per-task k1/k2) dressed in probabilistic language rather than a rigorously justified approximation.

The covariance model Σ0|t ≈ (k/SNR)·I is asserted from qualitative observations ("nearly isotropic as t→0") without any quantitative validation against the true (or TMPD) covariance, and the scalar k is not derived but tuned per task, which undercuts the claim that this replaces 'heuristic choices' in existing solvers—the paper essentially reintroduces a similarly heuristic hyperparameter to previous methods (analogous to λt in Eq. 14) despite claiming a principled advantage.

Table 4 shows highly task-specific hyperparameters (learning rate, k1, k2, gradient/annealing steps) that vary by an order of magnitude across tasks (e.g., k2 ranges from 0.01 to 30000); it is unclear how these were selected (validation set vs. test set) and whether comparable per-task tuning effort was afforded to baselines, raising concerns about a fair comparison protocol.

LMAPS is not uniformly best: it loses to SITCOM on several ImageNet tasks (SR, Nonlinear Deblurring) and to DDNM on Inpaint-Random for ImageNet, and the paper does not analyze or discuss these failure cases, weakening the 'state-of-the-art' framing implied by the abstract's headline PSNR gains, which appear cherry-picked from the tasks where LMAPS does best.

Baseline numbers for many methods are directly copied from DAPS/InverseBench rather than reproduced under the authors' own pipeline, so differences in evaluation details (exact NFE budgets, seeds, hardware) could confound the comparison, especially given the efficiency claims that depend sensitively on NFE accounting.

The relationship to very closely related concurrent work (Xu et al. 2025, arguing DPS is closer to MAP estimation, and Gutha et al. 2025, sampling the global MAP) is only briefly acknowledged in one sentence each in the related work section, without a clear technical contrast of what LMAPS adds beyond these existing MAP-oriented perspectives.

Minor presentation issues (repeated words, typos such as "0..01", inconsistent notation between H and \mathcal{H} across sections) suggest incomplete proofreading, and some Table 1 entries show implausible values (SSIM 0.467 for Quantization) that appear to be typographical errors, reducing confidence in the reported numbers.

strengths: Provides a clear conceptual framework (local MAP) that unifies and contextualizes existing DPS-family and optimization-based inverse problem solvers (TMPD, DiffPIR, DCDP, etc.), clarifying when local MAP coincides with DPS (Gaussian conditional case) and when it diverges (non-Gaussian/multimodal case), supported by an instructive analytic Gaussian-mixture toy example (Appendix A) that makes the mode-seeking bias explicit.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning 10 image restoration tasks (linear, nonlinear, non-differentiable) on FFHQ/ImageNet and 3 scientific inverse problems (LIS, CS-MRI, black hole imaging), with comparisons against ~15+ baselines, showing consistent PSNR/SSIM improvements and often better computational efficiency (fewer NFEs) than strong baselines like DAPS and SITCOM.

Reasonably rigorous supporting analysis: formal propositions (Appendix B) proving that the posterior covariance of x0 given xt is asymptotically isotropic as t→0, motivating the proposed covariance approximation; a temperature interpretation of the extra hyperparameter k (Appendix C) that adds some principled grounding.

Thorough ablations, including optimization-step vs. NFE trade-offs (Fig. 4), analytical vs. gradient-descent solutions (Table 8), and the effect of the measurement-conditioning strength k2 (Table 10), which help validate design choices and reproducibility of the method.

Transparent and detailed discussion of the relationship to the closely related concurrent work DMAP, explicitly delineating the difference between clean-signal-space and latent-space local MAP formulations.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to DMAP (Xu et al., 2025), which the paper itself describes as 'the closest related work' with 'the same high-level motivation.' The core contribution is largely a change of variable (clean-signal space vs. latent space) plus a covariance approximation and objective reformulation, rather than a fundamentally new inference paradigm, which may be seen as a modest contribution given ICML's bar for originality.

The isotropic covariance approximation is justified only asymptotically (as σ_t^2→0, i.e., near the end of the trajectory), yet it is applied uniformly across the entire diffusion trajectory including large-t regimes where the higher-order anisotropic terms are not necessarily negligible; the paper does not empirically quantify the approximation error at large t.

The additional hyperparameters (k, k1, k2, learning rate, gradient steps) require per-task tuning (Table 4 shows very different values across tasks, e.g., k2 ranging from 0.01 to 30000), undermining the claimed 'interpretability and numerical stability' benefits and raising concerns about practical usability and fair comparison to baselines that use fewer/simpler heuristics.

FID scores are frequently worse than several baselines (including DMAP) despite improved PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, reflecting the well-known reconstruction-vs-realism trade-off of MAP-style estimators; this trade-off is acknowledged only briefly and not analyzed quantitatively (e.g., no diversity or calibration metrics beyond the 2D toy example).

Some baseline numbers appear to be taken directly from other papers (DAPS, InverseBench) rather than being rerun under a controlled, unified experimental protocol, which raises reproducibility and fair-comparison concerns given that hyperparameter tuning and hardware can materially affect reported numbers.

The paper's central theoretical claim—that local MAP is 'a trade-off' between global MAP and posterior sampling—is stated qualitatively but not rigorously quantified (e.g., no bound on the distance between local MAP outputs and either the true posterior samples or the global MAP), leaving the main conceptual contribution somewhat informal.
Minor presentation issues (e.g., typo '0..01' in Table 4, dense notation, some repeated baseline/metric paragraphs verbatim in Sections 5.1/5.2) slightly detract from clarity and polish.
